extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or advanced-high-school students learning calculus and classical geometry; readers solving geometric extremum/constrained-optimization problems
extracted.subtask_description: Finding and characterizing extrema (maxima/minima/stationary points) of geometric quantities — distances, sums/differences of distances, angles, perimeters — under constraints (points on lines, closed curves, triangle sides), using elementary geometry and the differential calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: General tangency principle for extrema on a constraint curve
rubrics_metrics.description: If at a point R on a curve C a function f(x,y) has an extreme value a, the curve f(x,y)=a is tangent to C at R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument via the family of level curves f(x,y)=c: as c varies the level curves 'sweep' the plane; the extremal level curve that passes through R must leave C entirely on one side, hence be tangent at R. This principle is used to reduce constrained extremum problems to tangency conditions between level sets and the constraint curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse tangent / equal-angle property for sum of distances
rubrics_metrics.description: A tangent to an ellipse makes equal angles with the lines joining the foci to the point of tangency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking extrema of p+q (sum of distances to fixed points P and Q) on a curve C, consider the confocal ellipses p+q=2a. The extremal ellipse through the extremizing point R must be tangent to C; hence PR and QR make equal angles with the tangent to C at R. This furnishes both a characterization and a constructive tool (use ellipses to locate extrema).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola tangent / bisector property for difference of distances
rubrics_metrics.description: A tangent to a hyperbola at any point bisects the angle subtended at that point by the foci of the hyperbola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For extrema of p−q (difference of distances) consider level curves p−q=c — these are confocal hyperbolas. The extremal hyperbola tangent to the constraint C at R implies PR and QR make equal angles with the tangent there (i.e., the tangent bisects the angle between PR and QR). Distinguish cases when the points are on same or opposite sides of C and when C is closed vs a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection method for extrema on a straight line
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect one focus across the line L (P → P*). For points R on L, distances satisfy p = R P* (after reflection); extremizing p+q or |p−q| on L reduces to straight-line distance properties between P* and Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection to convert constrained problems on a line into unconstrained straight-line distance problems: the minimum of p+q occurs where the straight segment P*Q crosses L (giving equal-angle condition), and analogous constructions yield maxima of |p−q|. Caveats: if L is the perpendicular bisector of PQ some problems are degenerate (p−q=0 for all R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicularity condition for extreme distance from a point to a curve
rubrics_metrics.description: A point R on C where the distance PR is smallest or largest must satisfy that PR is perpendicular to the tangent to C at R (i.e., PR is normal to C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric proof: the circle centered at P passing through R must be tangent to C (otherwise points inside/outside the circle give smaller/larger distances), and the radius is perpendicular to the circle's tangent; hence PR ⟂ tangent to C. Applies equally to shortest and longest distances to a simple closed curve; analogous statements hold for endpoints of longest chord (diameter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of extrema on closed curves (extreme-value compactness principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a continuous quantity (e.g., p+q or p−q) on a closed curve C, both minimum and maximum values exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because C is a finite closed curve, the continuous function attains its greatest and least values on C (contrast with infinite lines where maxima may not exist). This justifies searching for tangent/normal conditions rather than worrying about nonexistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level-curve / contour method for constrained extrema (geometric foundation of Lagrange multipliers)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find extrema of f(x,y) subject to g(x,y)=0, consider the family of level curves f(x,y)=c; at an extremum the level curve is tangent to the constraint g=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric sweeping argument: the extremal level curve that first/last meets the constraint must touch it (no crossing), so tangency occurs. This yields the condition that gradients are parallel in analytic language. Examples: angle subtended by PQ (level curves are circles through P and Q), and earlier ellipse/hyperbola examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary-point condition in one-variable calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: At a maximum or minimum of a smooth function y=f(x) the tangent is horizontal, so f'(x)=0; points where f'(x)=0 are called stationary points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: f'(x)=0 is necessary but not sufficient for extrema: stationary points include relative/absolute maxima and minima and 'flat' points that are neither (example points A–E). Use higher-derivative tests or further analysis to classify stationary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary points, saddle points, and classification in several variables
rubrics_metrics.description: For z=f(x,y), maxima/minima correspond to peaks/valleys where the tangent plane is horizontal; saddle points (mountain passes) also have horizontal tangent planes but are neither max nor min.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize surfaces and contour maps: maxima/minima are surrounded by closed contours; saddle points are where contour lines cross. The tangent-plane-horizontal condition (vanishing first partials / gradient zero) yields candidate stationary points; further classification requires analysis of second derivatives (Morse theory mentioned for higher-dimensional topology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicular endpoints for longest chord (diameter) of a closed curve
rubrics_metrics.description: The diameter (longest chord) of a simple closed curve must be perpendicular to the curve at both endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from the perpendicularity condition for extreme distances to a curve; left as an exercise in the text. Similar statements can be formulated in higher dimensions (e.g., surfaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz's equal-angle/reflection condition for minimal inscribed triangle
rubrics_metrics.description: The inscribed triangle of least perimeter in an acute triangle is the altitude triangle; at each vertex of this minimal triangle the two sides make equal angles with the side of the original triangle (each such angle equals the opposite vertex angle of the original triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two complementary proofs given: (a) reflection proof — successive reflections produce six congruent triangles and show the altitude triangle has minimal perimeter; (b) use of earlier equal-angle criterion for sum of distances on a line to deduce equal-angle property at each contact point. Uniqueness, calculation of its perimeter, and exceptions for obtuse/right triangles are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case rule for obtuse triangles (degenerate minimizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the original triangle is obtuse, the altitude triangle does not minimize perimeter; instead the infimum is attained by twice the shortest altitude (a degenerate 'inscribed triangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: some feet of altitudes lie outside the triangle, making the altitude triangle not a proper inscribed triangle with minimal perimeter. The boundary (right-triangle) case coincides with both solutions. The altitude triangle still yields a stationary value of a minimax type for certain expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical / billiard reflection criterion and light-triangle stationarity
rubrics_metrics.description: In reflection problems (optics, billiards) a polygonal path that is stationary (e.g., extremal length or closed reflective path) is characterized by the property that at each reflection point the incoming and outgoing segments make equal angles with the boundary (law of reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'light triangle' is one whose sides make equal angles with the boundary at their endpoints; such triangles correspond to stationary values of total length with respect to vertex positions and may be minima, maxima, or mixed stationary types. Examples: elliptical billiard trajectories reflect foci-to-foci due to ellipse equal-angle property; rectangular billiard often leads to ergodic behavior; eight types of light triangles (combinatorics of max/min choices) are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting behavior of |p−q| along an infinite line and projection length
rubrics_metrics.description: For P and Q relative to an infinite line L, if no finite maximum of |p−q| exists (e.g., when P and Q are equidistant from L), the quantity |p−q| tends toward the length s of the perpendicular projection of PQ onto L as R → ∞ along L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains nonexistence of maxima in some line problems and gives the limiting value (exercise suggested). It distinguishes closed-curve cases (where maxima exist) from infinite-line cases.
